Addressing these shared biases is challenging because observational judge outputs alone cannot distinguish agreement driven by target quality from agreement driven by nuisance attributes. We introduce VoirDire, an intervention-calibrated aggregation method for LLM-judge panels. VoirDire applies controlled interventions that vary specified surface attributes while aiming to preserve the evaluation target; it then uses paired changes in judge scores to identify nuisance-sensitive directions. It attenuates these directions and selects aggregation weights that retain variation across items while penalizing sensitivity to the interventions, making the final consensus less dependent on superficial features. We show theoretically that observational judge outputs alone cannot identify which shared direction is target-relevant, while paired interventions provide the contrast needed to identify nuisance-sensitive variation. We evaluate VoirDire on 12 datasets spanning continuous scoring, binary classification, and pairwise preference. Compared with the existing LLM-judge aggregation baselines, VoirDire reduces MAE by up to 26.8% on continuous-score tasks and improves accuracy by up to 5.3 percentage points on binary and preference tasks. These findings suggest that counterfactual interventions provide an additional means of improving the reliability and controllability of LLM-based evaluation beyond merely relying on observed judge agreement.

title: Integer-Exact Microscaling: Running MXFP4 Language Models on INT8 Matrix Units
summary: On hardware whose fastest matrix datapath is INT8$\times$INT8, such as the Neural Accelerators of Apple's M5 GPUs, 4-bit weights must become INT8 operands. Existing MXFP4 kernels already map FP4 (E2M1) values to integers by doubling them, but apply every 32-element block scale inside the reduction. We show when no per-block work is needed: a row of MXFP4 weights is exactly one INT8 vector times one power-of-two scale if its block exponents span at most three, so a linear layer becomes a single INT8 GEMM with one rescale per output. Enforcing the condition adds at most 1/16 of a row's largest rounding error to the blocks it changes, and real weights already satisfy it: 97.9-99.97% of rows across seven models, including 99.93% of the 95M rows of a 125B-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next. The resulting spread-constrained MXFP4 files stay standard MXFP4. With integer instead of power-of-two block multipliers, an integer-exact format (16-wide blocks, multipliers 1..10, 4.26 bits) runs as one exact INT8 GEMM and is more accurate than NVFP4 (4.5 bits) with its standard scale rule on five small models, within 0.06 perplexity of NVFP4 with scale search. On Qwen3.8-Flash-Next's routed experts with INT8 activations it is as close to the FP8 model as NVFP4 with scale search (KL divergence 0.0557 vs. 0.0553) and closer than MLX's MXFP4 and affine INT4; with every matrix quantized it solves 94.8% of GSM8K vs. 91.0% for MLX's MXFP4. Quantizing only the 74k routed expert matrices (96% of the parameters) to either of our formats with INT8 activations costs at most 0.2% perplexity. A complete W4A8 system on the M5 produces outputs bit-identical to the quantized reference; prefill is 1.34-1.74x faster than MLX on a dense model, 1.10-1.57x on two MoE models up to 35B parameters and 1.22-1.29x on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, where shared non-GEMM work bounds the gain.

title: Where Causal Discovery Breaks on Real Data: Measuring the Assumptions One Property at a Time
summary: Causal discovery is usually evaluated on simulators or on systems whose ground truth follows from physics or design. When it fails on other real data, the failure is attributed to assumptions that may not hold, but which ones fail, and by how much, is rarely measured. We measure the observable properties of the data they bear on, one property at a time, on a real panel. The case study follows 2,901 US public firms over 31 quarters, with 71 types of corporate action from SEC 8-K filings, 11 financial-statement items, and an expert graph over 651 action-state pairs. The panel breaks measurable requirements of discovery: tails that survive winsorisation, balance-sheet items and revenue close to random walks, and interventions too rare to detect effects of a tenth of a standard deviation in 40 of 71 actions. Even so, a marginal test ranks expert-labelled direct above not-direct pairs within each action (AUROC 0.658) better than every null we built, so the panel does carry information about which pairs are direct. Tuned discovery methods, in configurations feasible at this panel size, recover less of it than a simple pairwise cross-correlation when pairs are ranked within each action, and no more when they are ranked within each target, which removes what the target alone predicts. Most direct pairs (132 of 222) involve actions below the support needed for 80% power against a 0.1-SD effect. For flow targets, conditioning on the target's other expert-labelled parents, often filed alongside the action, erodes the marginal discrimination, and most not-direct associations survive it: even with the graph's parent sets supplied, the expected separation does not emerge. For each property, we give a diagnostic computable before any discovery method is run.

title: A Straight Line Is Not a Camera Pose: Auditing Short-Clip Pose Benchmarks
comment: 34 pages (8-page main text and appendix), 7 figures, 21 tables
summary: The absolute trajectory error (ATE) is the standard measure of camera-motion accuracy, from SLAM to feed-forward 3D reconstruction. On the common Sintel protocol, a constant-velocity straight line using no images has a lower mean ATE than 10 of 11 recent models re-run with official code. Two properties of ATE's alignment explain this. First, it maps any constant-velocity prediction onto the best-fitting line through the true path, so the line scores the path's regression residual. A residual signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) criterion predicts when moving a prediction towards its constant-velocity fit lowers ATE. It gives the outcome for 95% of 1056 model-clip pairs, 98% of 792 held-out pairs and 97% of 1034 ScanNet pairs, and it separates Sintel (median SNR 0.86) from TUM, ScanNet and full-length Bonn and Wild-SLAM (2.7 to 27), where straightening raises every model's mean ATE. Second, position-only alignment ignores where cameras look: rotating a trajectory by 30 degrees against its orientations leaves ATE unchanged, yet worsens the reprojection of static points for every model on Sintel, TUM and ScanNet in the main setting, and the line, second by mean ATE on Sintel, places them worst by geometric mean: a lower ATE need not mean better geometry. Fitting the alignment's rotation to the predicted orientations gives pose-anchored ATE, a one-function change in ATE's units costing 0.17 ms per clip (ATE: 0.11 ms). It ranks every image-free reference below every model on Sintel, tracks the reprojection error under rotation and straightening, where ATE does not (Spearman 0.61 vs. 0.32), largely preserves the models' order, and ties 10-frame translational relative pose error (RPE) and the discernible trajectory error (DTE) on our rotation and reference tests. Code, predictions and results will be released.

title: Spatial Uncertainty Analytics for Budget-Limited Inspection of Hyperspectral Scenes
summary: Land-cover maps classified from wide-area hyperspectral surveys are least reliable along class boundaries and in ambiguous regions, so their errors are spatially structured. We study how this structure can direct a limited verification budget: when a low-altitude UAV or a ground crew can visit only a handful of sites, where it should go depends on how classifier uncertainty is arranged across the scene and how a fixed sensor footprint tiles that arrangement. We estimate a per-pixel uncertainty surface from the disagreement of an ensemble of spectral classifiers and select sites by greedy, field-of-view-aware coverage of the uncertainty mass. On seven benchmark scenes, the highest-uncertainty decile of pixels is 2.6 to 7.9 times richer in errors than the scene as a whole, and the coverage greedy covers up to 57% of the classifier's errors with 15 sites, 1.7 to 18 times as many as uncertainty-agnostic sampling of the same labelled region. A non-overlapping selection of the footprints richest in uncertainty does equally well, so the gain comes from scoring whole footprints by uncertainty mass. The advantage persists under spatially blocked evaluation and with a spectral-spatial classifier, although disagreement then ranks errors less well. It requires restricting the surface to labelled land cover: over the whole scene, disagreement peaks on unlabelled ground, where inspections cannot be scored. The best policy for covering connected high-uncertainty regions depends on the scene and on the threshold that defines them, and Gaussian-process selection covers less uncertainty than the coverage greedy on every scene. The pipeline runs on commodity CPUs.

title: Ensemble Classification and Cancer-Specific Gene Signatures from Quality-Aware Hybrid Gene Selection in TCGA RNA-Seq data
comment: 17 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables and 1 supplementary file
summary: Gene-expression classifiers of cancer type are usually developed and validated within one cohort using random splits. Starting from a quality-aware hybrid Boruta selector from earlier work, we developed and evaluated ensemble classifiers and cancer-specific gene signatures. Using 10,469 TCGA tumours of 33 types, we compared five learners and three ensembles under decision rules fixed in advance, reran the selection in site-grouped cross-validation, transferred a breast-cancer subtype panel to 3273 tumours of the independent SCAN-B cohort, and built five-gene stage~I tumour versus adjacent-normal panels for nine cancer types. Logistic regression (LR) was the most accurate and best-calibrated single learner (balanced accuracy 0.943 on the locked test set). Stacking added at most 0.006 with 1000 genes but improved on LR in every fold with a minimal 100-gene panel; a hierarchical model did not reduce within-group confusion. Site-grouped validation lowered balanced accuracy by 0.027, almost entirely in colon and rectal cancer (0.008 without them and the untestable LAML). On SCAN-B, the subtype panel reached 0.855, close to the 50 PAM50 genes (0.876). Stage~I panels reached ROC AUC >= 0.99 in held-out patients and detected most later-stage tumours. Ensembles help most with a minimal panel; with 1000 genes, a calibrated linear model suffices.

title: Few Trials, Many Metrics: Beta Mixtures for Low-Budget AI Evaluation
summary: Evaluating a stochastic AI system often requires many repeated samples per instance, especially for metrics defined over long horizons. Recent work has shown that modeling instance-level success probabilities with a Beta distribution recovers Pass@$k$ from far fewer samples than direct estimation. We show that this framework supports a broader range of evaluation targets. We fit a mixture of Beta distributions by marginal maximum likelihood, with the number of components chosen by BIC. From that one fit, we compute Pass$^k$ and AUC@$k$ at any horizon in closed form. We also derive delta-method confidence intervals for these metrics and for Pass@$k$, which require no additional model calls. Treating configurations rather than tasks as instances extends the same model to sensitivity analysis. For repeated success metrics, we find that mixture priors yield more accurate estimators than naive estimation across competition mathematics and graduate-level science benchmarks when extrapolating beyond the observed number of trials, and the resulting intervals cover the full-data reference. When prompts are treated as instances, it estimates the distribution of prompt sensitivity more accurately than a comparable item-response baseline without external covariates. Direct estimators remain preferable once trials reach the target horizon.

title: Stochastic learning flow: moment equations for stochastic gradient descent at finite step size
summary: Analytical theories of learning in deep networks often assume gradient flow, discarding the finite step size and batch noise of stochastic gradient descent (SGD). Starting from the discrete update, we derive continuous-time equations for the mean and covariance of the parameter distribution under a Gaussian closure for a general stochastic learning, to first order in the learning rate $η$. Applying these stochastic learning flow (SLF) equations to SGD, we show that the mean descends an effective loss regularized by the covariance and loss curvature, while the covariance, unlike in stochastic differential equation approximations, becomes unstable at curvature $2/η$. In SGD ensembles of linear and nonlinear networks, SLF predicts learning curves and mean trajectories more accurately than gradient flow and captures the covariance dynamics, failing where the parameter distribution becomes strongly non-Gaussian. In the full-batch limit, the edge of stability corresponds to a stationary point of the coupled sharpness-covariance dynamics, recovering self-stabilization and central flow, and batch-to-batch curvature fluctuations lower this threshold under SGD.

title: Compression Technique Interactions in Small Language Models: A Factorial Ablation Study
summary: Deploying small language models on resource-constrained hardware requires compression, yet practitioners lack systematic guidance on how quantization, pruning, and post-compression recovery interact when combined. We present a factorial ablation study evaluating 72 compression configurations across four SLM architectures (2.7B-7B parameters), extended with a 48-configuration ordering analysis, benchmark accuracy validation on 30 compressed models, and robustness checks including multi-seed validation and full-corpus perplexity evaluation. INT8 quantization is effectively lossless (<0.5% accuracy degradation), while NF4 quantization combined with L1 magnitude pruning causes model collapse in all 16 tested combinations. LoRA-based fine-tuning reduces degraded perplexity by up to 97% after aggressive pruning; an ablation against standard fine-tuning without a teacher model shows the recovery is driven by LoRA adaptation itself rather than the distillation signal. Compression ordering shows no significant effect among viable configurations (ANOVA p = 0.96) but determines viability for NF4+pruning combinations. INT8 quantization alone provides 40-45% memory reduction with no quality loss. On-device CPU deployment via llama.cpp confirms these findings transfer off the GPU: 4-bit quantization runs 46-54% faster than 8-bit for a perplexity difference under 0.5 points, while un-structured pruning yields no CPU latency or memory benefit, consistent with its dense storage format.

title: Exo: An Architecture for Self-Improving Systems at Runtime
summary: Agent harnesses govern how language models act in an environment; designing their policies by hand is difficult, while automated techniques require representative datasets and costly executions. We present Exo, an agent runtime architecture for safe learning during ongoing work that collapses the optimization loop into task execution, allowing agents to revise both their harness and their strategies for further improvement. A minimal protected mechanism layer preserves execution history and governs policy activation while the harness evolves through inspectable code changes. On long-running objectives in an open-world game, Exo reduces model cost by 12-53% relative to Codex and Pi in standalone runs and 45-82% in transfer runs, while matching task completion rates. Compared with the same starting policy without the ability to edit policy, Exo reduces held-out model cost by 35-61% on AppWorld and SREGym with comparable correctness, cutting AppWorld's mean task time by 13% and SREGym's median diagnosis time by 35%. On Continual Learning Bench coding tasks, model cost including learning falls by 14%, with both policies resolving every issue.

title: From Small to Large: Assessing Medical Reasoning, Benchmark Contamination, and Model Size in Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) now answer medical exam questions at or above expert level, but it is unclear whether such scores reflect clinical competence, or are instead affected by the format of the questions being asked (e.g., multiple-choice versus open-ended), prior exposure to the benchmarks, and the difficulty of the questions. These benchmarks are also public and widely used online, which may be resulting in LLM memorization. Models may perform better on questions that they have seen before. It is also not evident whether smaller models, which are more locally deployable in HIPAA-compliant hospital settings, have achieved human performance. In this study, we evaluate fourteen current models from six leading providers, one smaller and one larger model from each provider with two additional open-weight models, on 3,076 questions from four medical benchmarks (MedQA-USMLE, MedMCQA, PubMedQA, and MedBullets) under standard multiple choice, the same questions with the answer choices withheld, and reconstruction of a hidden question from its choices alone. In the standard multiple-choice setting, the strongest models exceed the human-expert baseline on MedQA-USMLE and PubMedQA, but the smaller models trail their larger models by 8.7 percentage points and only two of the six pass the human-expert bar on the licensing examination. Withholding the answer choices, however, makes every model struggle: mean accuracy falls from 82.3% to 50.9%, and the two largest drops belong to the medically specialised models. On memorization, the strongest models reconstruct one question in four from the answer choices alone, yet accuracy holds on the questions they cannot reconstruct. We further weigh accuracy against inference cost and test whether ensembling several models improves medical question answering.

title: PRISM-Net: Dynamic Routing Network with VLM-Guided Disentangled Attribute Distillation for Explainable Fine-Grained Product Retrieval
summary: Fine-grained visual product retrieval in large-scale e-commerce multimedia systems demands discriminative representations capable of simultaneously resolving macro-level category semantics and micro-level visual attributes such as structural contour (line) and chromatic appearance (color). However, conventional backbones including convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and vision Transformers (ViTs) inherently suffer from feature entanglement and shortcut learning. To learn the micro-level visual attributes without costly manual attribute annotations, we propose phase-routed interpretable semantic mixture-of-experts network (PRISM-Net), an explainable multi-expert architecture that disentangles holistic visual features into disentangled line and color expert pathways governed by a conditional meta-router. In phase 1, we introduce an external VLM-Guided sigmoid semantic distillation mechanism with gradient-detached routing gates, utilizing zero-shot text prompts from SigLIP to supervise specialized structural and chromatic experts. In phase 2, the disentangled expert embeddings are adaptively fused with macro base features via a learned meta-router gate to calibrate category boundaries. Extensive 5-fold cross-validation across 275,454 e-commerce images (18 categories) and full-scale retrieval benchmarks (55,091 queries against a 220,363-image gallery) across SwinV2, ConvNeXt-V2, and DINOv3 demonstrate substantial gains. On SwinV2, PRISM-Net boosts full-fold product mAP@10 from 80.98% to 83.90% (+2.92%), line mAP@10 by +5.74%, and color mAP@10 by +9.12%. Furthermore, unsupervised distribution analysis of the meta-router gate reveals that both ViT and CNN backbones emergently allocate up to 6.8x higher structural line weights to rigid appliances and hardware while dedicating >96% chromatic weight to clothing.

title: Compositional Self-Improvement: Promises and Pitfalls
summary: Although self-improvement is becoming increasingly important as tasks become more complex, models struggle to generate reliable supervision for harder, out-of-distribution instances. One way to address this challenge is to exploit compositional structure: models often solve simpler subproblems more reliably than full problems, so their subproblem predictions can be composed into supervision for harder ones. We systematically study when this kind of composed supervision supports self-improvement and when it fails. Our controlled experiments identify three failure modes: unreliable subproblem predictions, errors introduced by composition, and limited supervision coverage. Beyond controlled settings, these findings carry over to more realistic coding and reasoning tasks: composed labels are more accurate than direct self-generated labels and improve performance even on compositions longer than those seen during training, while the failure modes remain visible. Further, although these failure modes often keep compositional self-improvement from fully succeeding on its own, a short SFT warmup with compositional self-improvement can bootstrap reinforcement learning on tasks that require composing skills the model already has, particularly when direct exploration rarely succeeds. Together, these findings characterize when compositional self-improvement can provide sufficiently reliable supervision to expand model capabilities.

title: Learning to evolve by matching velocities
summary: Learning the continuous-time evolution of nonlinear dynamical systems relies on trajectory-based objectives, which require simulating the learned dynamics during training and backpropagating through the numerical scheme, at a cost that grows with the rollout horizon. We show that trajectory-based objectives degenerate as the rollout horizon increases, hindering gradient-based optimization, and that the numerical scheme biases the learned dynamics by constraining the spectrum of the learned Jacobian to its absolute stability region. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Velocity Matching (VM), a simulation-free objective that relies on piecewise-linear interpolation and stochastic collocation, and approximates the velocity population risk to second order in the sampling step. We develop a theoretical framework for velocity-based learning, introducing stability estimates that control trajectory errors in terms of velocity errors, which enable us to establish universal and continuous-time approximation results when the learned velocity field is parameterized by deep neural networks. Building on a bias-variance decomposition of the VM objective, we show that its higher-order approximation of the velocity population risk yields a consistent minimizer; that it relates to the residual of an A-stable continuous-stage Runge-Kutta scheme, thus connecting VM to implicit integration without requiring any implicit solve; and that it implicitly matches the action of the learned Jacobian to that of the true one along the observed trajectories, without requiring access to the underlying velocity field or its Jacobian. Numerical experiments on nonlinear ordinary differential equations and semi-discretized time-dependent partial differential equations show that VM improves accuracy over trajectory-based objectives, while avoiding both the cost of simulation and the instabilities of long rollouts.

title: Quantiles, Not Points: Streaming Quantile Matching for Ordinal-Aware LLM-as-a-Judge Calibration
summary: LLM-as-a-judge scores are often distributionally shifted from human ratings on any given evaluation task, and post-hoc calibration (mapping LLM to human scores in a small labeled anchor set) has become a popular method to correct for this shift. In this paper we derive the calibration from two positions: that LLMaJ scores are ordinal ratings drawn from a distribution rather than isolated points. We present streaming quantile matching (SQM), a version of a classical method not previously bench marked for LLMaJ calibration, which is built on the two positions by computing the optimal-transport map between the LLM and human score distributions. We develop an evaluation framework and within it we show that unlike point-wise calibrations, SQM respects the ordinality of the human anchor set and achieves the best distributional fidelity and the top overall rank across models and data. We also show that in general, post-hoc calibration narrows the raw error gap between smaller and larger judge models, which opens the possibility of more efficient LLM judges.

title: CLiS: Plug-and-Play Attention Acceleration for Video Diffusion on TPUs via Certified Stabilization
summary: High-resolution video diffusion relies on attention over long token sequences, making attention efficiency critical to generation latency. Our analysis identifies repeated maximum reductions and accumulator rescaling in online softmax as a bottleneck in long-context TPU attention. We propose CLiS (Certified Loop-invariant Stabilization), a training-free, plug-and-play optimization for video diffusion inference. CLiS fixes per-row stabilizers before the KV loop and certifies numerical safety per head, falling back to online softmax when certification fails. It integrates into existing fused-attention kernels without changing model weights or architecture. On Wan 2.2 and LTX-2 across TPU v6e and TPU7x, CLiS reduces diffusion transformer (DiT) step latency by up to 19.6% relative to tuned online softmax without measurable quality loss. Controlled TPU adaptations of prior GPU stabilization methods show performance or numerical-safety limitations. Preliminary causal LLM experiments also show up to 13.5% higher training throughput in continued pretraining and 7.7% in supervised fine-tuning.

title: OmniMechanism Design for Human-AI Collaboration with Impressionable Minds
summary: As AI systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, effectively integrating human expertise with AI outputs is critical for reliable decision-making. A substantial body of theoretical work studies optimal mechanisms for human-AI collaboration (HAC), focusing on when to involve humans and how to combine their expertise with AI predictions. However, these approaches largely overlook a key factor highlighted by empirical evidence: human judgments are impressionable and can vary depending on how AI outputs are presented. For example, when AI systems defer decisions to humans, revealing or withholding the AI prediction can significantly influence human judgments. Moreover, existing work neglects deployment-time variability, where conditions, particularly the cost of eliciting human input, may differ substantially from those observed during training. To address these challenges, we introduce a rigorous and theoretically grounded framework for human-AI collaboration, termed collaborative omnimechanism design, based on a novel and computationally efficient contextual bandit variant of boosting for outcome indistinguishability. In particular, we reduce a calibration-type outcome indistinguishability condition to weighted calibration, providing a novel time-efficiency result, bypassing the high-dimension curse induced by complicated collaboration methods and outcome space. Our framework provides a principled characterization of human impressionability and introduces a unified optimization scheme that enables robust and adaptable decision-making across diverse query costs and evaluation objectives without retraining. We evaluate the framework in three HAC settings, examining adaptation to query costs and prediction objectives without retraining, and show that its induced policies perform comparably to or better than the evaluated baselines.

title: Statistical Inference under Performativity: From Policy Feedback to Self-Evolving Systems
comment: Extended version of the NeurIPS 2025 paper "Statistical Inference under Performativity" (arXiv:2505.18493)
summary: Performativity arises when prediction-informed decisions change the data-generating process, creating feedback between deployment and learning. This phenomenon occurs in policy-making and in self-evolving AI systems that shape their own future training data. Statistical inference is challenging because estimation errors in earlier predictors affect subsequent data distributions and propagate into later updates. We develop an end-to-end framework for statistical inference under performativity. For repeated risk minimization and repeated gradient descent, we establish central limit theorems at fixed deployment rounds and derive covariance recursions that capture both current-round sampling variation and uncertainty inherited from earlier deployments. We develop consistent covariance estimators using policy perturbations and score matching. These results can yield asymptotically valid confidence regions for population iterates and the performative stable point. We further extend prediction-powered inference to this dynamic setting, combining labeled observations with predictions on additional unlabeled data to improve statistical efficiency. We evaluate our framework in synthetic, semi-synthetic educational, and self-evolving large language model routing settings. Our experiments demonstrate that ignoring propagated uncertainty can lead to substantial undercoverage even after repeated retraining. Together, these results provide statistical tools for learning systems that help determine the distributions from which they learn. Our work establish a complete statistical inference under performativity, introducing new challenges and inference settings that we believe will provide substantial value to policy-making, statistics, and machine learning.

title: Local Spatial TreeSHAP: Geographically Explainable AI Revealing Urbanization-Dependent Spatial Heterogeneity in Flood Resilience
summary: Urban flood resilience emerges from complex interactions among natural, built, and socio-economic systems, yet most recovery policies implicitly assume that resilience mechanisms are spatially uniform. To address this gap, this study develops a spatially explainable machine learning framework that integrates geographically weighted random forests with a novel Local Spatial TreeSHAP algorithm, enabling nonlinear resilience mechanisms to be identified and interpreted at the community scale. The framework is applied to 779 communities affected by the July 2023 extreme rainstorm in Beijing. Results reveal that resilience mechanisms exhibit substantially stronger spatial heterogeneity than the underlying physical and socio-economic conditions themselves, with SHAP-value spatial autocorrelation decreasing by 66.2% on average relative to predictor variables. Three distinct resilience regimes emerge across the urbanization gradient. Highly urbanized communities benefit from synergistic interactions among commercial infrastructure and accommodation services; transitional medium urbanized communities are constrained by infrastructure-development mismatches that create facility gaps despite continued urban expansion; and low urbanized communities are dominated by ecological and topographic thresholds, where adverse interactions between transportation and river-network structures undermine recovery capacity. Field investigations and interviews with 12 stakeholders corroborate these patterns. By linking geographically weighted machine learning with locally grounded attribution analysis, the proposed framework provides a new pathway for uncovering spatially varying resilience mechanisms and translating them into place-based recovery strategies under increasing climate extremes.

title: Real-VAS: a Real-World Video Amodal Segmentation Dataset
comment: 34 pages, including supplementary material. Project page: https://finlay-hudson.github.io/real_vas
summary: Amodal video object segmentation is fundamentally limited by the absence of datasets that combine real-world complexity with precise ground-truth annotations. To address this, we present Real Video Amodal Segmentation (Real-VAS), a new large-scale, zero-shot evaluation dataset built from composited real-image video. We introduce a novel data generation pipeline that enables the creation of programmatically consistent amodal ground truth for real-world footage, in which the object mask, occlusion boundary, and composited image are all derived from a single unoccluded source, without relying on human estimation or expensive 3D reconstruction. Our dataset is structured into two challenging scenarios: dynamic Occlusion, created by compositing two clips of moving objects, and a unique Container category featuring complex, physically constrained interactions. These container scenarios--On Surface Containment, Articulated Containment, and Mobile Containment--allow us to generate precise ground truth by simulating an object's motion based on its container's tracked transformation. As a result, Real-VAS provides a diverse and challenging benchmark for evaluating amodal segmentation models on realistic video with the precision of synthetic data. The dataset and our generation code will be made publicly available.

title: Do Multimodal Models Decide Consistently on Equivalent Optical Spectra?
comment: 20 pages, 4 figures, 11 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/zwang-devv/spectra-decision-audit
summary: A spectrum can be given to a model as a table in nanometers or as a plot in photon energy, and the decision should not depend on which one it sees. When the data needed for an answer are missing, the model should say so. We test representation invariance and abstention on measured optical spectra of silicon metasurfaces (MOCLIP) and gold nanoparticles, with labels computed from the data. Each spectrum is shown as four tables (nm, $μ$m, scientific notation, eV) and two plots (nm, eV), and partial spectra remove data inside or outside the queried range. We evaluate the decision models d3-nano and Jev 1.13, three GPT-6 Luna configurations and the Qwen3.5-2B base model. Changing only the representation moves accuracy by up to 41 percentage points within one model, mostly on photon-energy tables and plots. With the same evidence, asking in photon energy instead of wavelength helps some model-view pairs by 16-50 points and hurts others by up to 25. When the relevant extremum is removed, unadapted models rarely answer "undetermined". LoRA fine-tuning of d3-nano improves comparisons on the trained table formats, but much of its gain on unanswerable questions comes from a shortcut: it abstains whenever the input is truncated. Training with answerable truncations avoids the shortcut in all six seeds, with a 90-100 point gap between abstention after inside and outside cuts on held-out structures; with the same amount of extra original-task data, five of six seeds keep the shortcut. On gold spectra the two training sets perform similarly. Multimodal language models used for scientific decisions should be tested on equivalent representations and on missing evidence, not only on average accuracy. We release the tasks, per-response results and analysis code.

title: Spoofing the Latent State: Imperceptible Goal-Image Attacks Derail Planning in LeWorldModel
summary: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) have recently emerged as general-purpose visual world models for control. A prominent example is LeWorldModel (LeWM), which trains end-to-end from pixels using an isotropic Gaussian anti-collapse regularizer (SIGReg) and plans by minimizing the squared Euclidean distance between predicted and goal embeddings. In this work, we investigate the test-time robustness of this latent planning interface. Analyzing the learned metric on Push-T, we first find that task-relevant object state heavily dominates latent distance: shifting the block by a single pixel displaces the embedding $3\times$ further than an equivalent agent shift, and swapping the block pose alone accounts for $99\%$ of the distance between scene pairs. However, because this pose information is distributed across a curved, high-dimensional manifold rather than a fixed linear subspace, the encoder cannot be trivially edited post-hoc to isolate or redirect it. We next demonstrate that this geometry is highly vulnerable at test time. A white-box $\ell_\infty$ perturbation of just $ε{=}4/255$ applied to a single input frame causes the encoder to register the block at an arbitrary, attacker-chosen pose in $73$--$95\%$ of scenes without disturbing the encoded agent state. Perturbing either the goal image or the live camera observation drops Push-T planning success from $87\%$ to $32\%$, whereas uniform random noise at twice the magnitude has negligible impact. This vulnerability persists across all four standard LeWM benchmarks (Push-T, Two-Room, Reacher, and OGBench-Cube). At $ε{=}8/255$, the attack bridges $82$--$97\%$ of the squared latent distance to the target embedding in every environment, inducing planning degradation proportional to each task's reliance on the spoofed entity.

title: PAM-Mamba - Efficient Dense Action Detection using Mamba
summary: Dense action detection requires precisely localising multiple overlapping actions in long untrimmed videos. Transformer-based methods achieve strong accuracy but their $O(T^2)$ self-attention cost limits scalability. We present PAM-Mamba, a linear-time $O(T)$ architecture built on Mamba with a multi-branch temporal encoder. Gated Learnable Positional Encoding (GLPE) controls positional signal injection via a scalar gate initialised to zero, starting training without added positional signal. A Hub-and-Spoke Funnel extends the non-hierarchical multi-scale design of PAT with a direct residual from the original full-resolution input to each coarse branch, providing each coarse branch with a projection of the input features. Bi-TemBa (Bidirectional Temporal Mamba) first extracts local motion cues with a shallow Temporal Convolution Module, then applies a cascaded bidirectional Mamba scan; the backward pass refines the forward-scanned representation from the opposite direction, giving each temporal position access to context from both directions in linear time. Uncertainty-Based Mixup uses prediction entropy to guide the selection of mixup partners. Using the PAT evaluation implementation, we obtain 26.82 (Charades I3D), 34.59 (Charades CLIP), 46.56 (MultiTHUMOS I3D), and 46.92 mAP (MultiTHUMOS CLIP), with 26.1-27.9M parameters, 61-63% fewer than PAT.

title: A Spectral Renormalization-Group View of Learning
summary: We study how the layers in deep neural networks (NNs) converge, using Wilsonian Renormalization-Group (RG) ideas to organize the spectral picture. During training, these layers often develop heavy-tailed power-law (PL) spectra, and the strongest checkpoints often appear near the PL exponent $α\approx 2$. This pattern raises a simple question: why should this value mark a well-trained layer? The answer is both statistical and physical. Our statistical hypothesis is that $α=2$ marks the boundary between stable if not optimal learning and overfitting via non-self-averaging. The physical answer is that the same value makes the spectral energy gain scale evenly across logarithmic spectral scales, which is the proposed Wilsonian marginal condition. We then apply the ERG trace-log condition, the proposed SETOL theory, which we justify by taking volume-preserving, scale-invariant transformations to remove arbitrary layer scale along the proposed RG flow. The resulting spectral RG flow connects the HTSR and SETOL theories to optimizers such as Muon, and motivates a new optimizer extension, WW-PGD. Together, these results point toward a spectral Renormalization-Group view of learning, in which NNs may approach shared spectral structure in the settings studied here.

title: RankLane: Efficient MoE Prefill on Accelerators with Ranked Expert Capacities
summary: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models expand model capacity by activating only a subset of experts for each token. On accelerators with static execution plans, expert capacities and placement are fixed before routing reveals each expert's load. Uniform worst-case capacities waste work on padding; smaller capacities tied to expert identities can overflow. We present RankLane, which ranks each device's experts by current load and assigns them to fixed-capacity lanes. Runtime indices select experts and token rows while tier populations, shapes and device placement remain fixed. An aggregation graph preserves device ownership and reduces each token's local contributions on one core. Routing calibration and measured execution costs guide tier selection; overflowing chunks rerun at full capacity. We evaluate full-model prefill of Qwen3-30B-A3B and Gemma 4 26B-A4B with MXFP6 weights on four Cloud AI 100 Ultra SoCs, using 128-2048-token chunks and including overflow detection and in-program recovery support. Against a dense baseline, RankLane achieves end-to-end prefill speedups of 1.27-4.18x on Qwen3 and 1.93-3.46x on Gemma.

title: Nonconformal Distortion and Local Orientation Reversal in the Fourier Circuit of a Modular-Addition Transformer
summary: We study the local differential geometry of a Fourier-based modular-addition circuit in a one-layer transformer whose algorithm has previously been reverse-engineered. For each of the five key Fourier frequencies, we restrict the model's multilayer perceptron (MLP) contribution to a corresponding Fourier input plane and readout, and measure its directional Beltrami coefficient under continuous input perturbations. Whereas nondegenerate restrictions of ideal complex multiplication are conformal, the trained maps exhibit nonconformal distortion (median $|μ|=0.304$--$0.446$), spatial organization in the Beltrami argument, and regions of local orientation reversal. The median across frequencies decreases from $0.939$ at initialization to $0.390$ after training. The key-frequency planes also show lower median distortion than most random-plane controls, although their distributions overlap and the coordinate frames differ in conditioning. Across 500 checkpoints in one training run, most of the aggregate reduction in Beltrami magnitude occurs before the principal increase in the measured Fourier-circuit formation. At the individual-input level, Beltrami magnitude shows negligible association with the correct-logit margin ($|ρ|\leq0.026$). Late-checkpoint measurements across six runs show comparable distortion for most selected frequencies. These results provide a quantitative characterization of local deformation in a frequency-projected component of an identified neural circuit, complementary to its algorithmic reconstruction.

title: TileWeave: Heterogeneous Tiling for Sparse Prefill on Mobile SoCs
summary: Smartphone applications increasingly require large language models to process long contexts, whereas high prefill latency and memory demands constrain local inference. Block-sparse attention reduces computation and memory traffic, but its irregular selections conflict with mobile NPUs' preference for large, regular tiles. Efficient execution must exploit cross-query reuse while avoiding redundant computation and preserving selections needed for accuracy. In this paper, we present TileWeave, which partitions sparse attention by this cross-query reuse: highly shared key blocks run in coarse NPU tiles, while low-reuse blocks run on the GPU only for the query blocks that selected them. In addition, we design an NPU-native pooled-key selector that keeps selection inexpensive, and a runtime that publishes GPU partials in the order the NPU consumes them and merges them in its existing output store. On RULER, HeteroSparse matches XAttention's accuracy with Qwen3-1.7B and improves it with Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct; its mean LongBench scores match XAttention as well. On Snapdragon SM8750 and SM8850 phones, it achieves 1.35--3.23$\times$ faster full-model prefill than XAttention over 1k--16k tokens and up to 1.58$\times$ faster than dense attention.

title: Hacking or Just Failing? A More Capable LLM Monitor Better Separates Reward Hacking from Honest Failure
comment: 14 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables. Code, data and pre-registrations: https://github.com/KaushikKC/weak-monitor-lab
summary: An agent's visible score can exceed its real progress because it gamed the score or because it simply made mistakes, so a useful reward-hacking monitor must tell the two apart. We built a sandboxed task in which an agent can game a completion score, labelled every episode by replaying it and repairing the final state counterfactually, and ran five pre-registered studies. On 60 episodes from a Llama 3.1 8B agent, small local monitors (Llama 3B and 8B) did not separate exploit attempts from honest failures with the same score gap: prompt changes traded missed exploits for false alarms, and the pre-registered primary monitor reached AUC 0.64. On identical inputs, Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite, which completed 9/10 clean tasks against 2/10 for the 8B model, met our pre-registered criterion (AUC 0.80, 95% interval [0.66, 0.93]; 1/35 honest failures flagged); with only 14 exploit episodes, this estimate is uncertain. On an exploit that no prompt names, Gemini usually described the action correctly yet never flagged it, in 5 and then 25 new episodes, even when manipulation was defined by its effect on the score. Given the full trace, the 8B monitor flagged all 25 replication episodes and none of 25 honest look-alikes, but its explanations described actions that had not occurred; given additional structured evidence, it also flagged 15 of the 25 look-alikes. A two-rule deterministic check caught every known exploit. We release the environment, labels, pre-registrations and per-judgement logs.

title: TAP-Out: Tracking Any Point in 360° via Outpainting
comment: Accepted at BMVC 2026. 22 pages, including supplementary material. Project page: https://finlay-hudson.github.io/tapout/
summary: Tracking points that leave the camera's field of view (FoV) requires reasoning about unobserved scene dynamics, a fundamentally different problem from tracking visible correspondences. We present TAP-Out, an offline method that makes this out-of-view (OOV) reasoning explicit by leveraging generative video outpainting as a world-model prior. Given a narrow-FoV input video, TAP-Out outpaints a complete 360° equirectangular video, locates target objects within the panoramic scene via video object segmentation, and synthesises object-centred perspective crops on which standard in-frame trackers operate. This decoupled design composes off-the-shelf foundation models without requiring task-specific architectural modifications. On the TAPVid360 benchmark, TAP-Out achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving OOV tracking accuracy by approximately 3x over the best prior method. We demonstrate its flexibility on out-of-frame object segmentation and detection and we provide detailed diagnostic analyses across motion regimes, static versus dynamic content, and hallucination quality, characterising when and why the approach succeeds or fails.

title: MXCode: Vector Quantization for MX-Native Inference at Scale
summary: Memory capacity and bandwidth are major bottlenecks in LLM inference, motivating weight compression beyond conventional 4-bit quantization. Vector quantization (VQ) enables approximately 2-bit weight storage but often relies on codebooks incompatible with native FP4 computation. We introduce MXCode (MX-Native Codebook Quantization), a framework bridging ultra-low-bit VQ compression with MicroXcaling (MX)-native FP4 computation. MXCode proposes three strategies: PostScale, which quantizes learned codebooks to MXFP4; PreScale, which extracts MX scales before codebook learning; and PreScale+, which further compresses these scales using VQ. These strategies explore tradeoffs among quantization quality, scale overhead, and codebook granularity. All reconstruct MX-native W4A4 operands without materializing intermediate high-precision weights. We evaluate MXCode on Qwen3 (235B), DeepSeek-R1 (671B), and GLM-5.2 (753B) using the Microsoft MX Emulation Library. MXCode achieves approximately 2 bits per weight with competitive, workload-dependent model quality. On GB300 hardware, experiments with Qwen3 (235B) show approximately 50% lower model-load memory than Native FP4 while maintaining near-Native-FP4 serving throughput. Under memory-constrained prefix reuse, P90 TTFT improves by up to 94.5%. These results demonstrate software-based reconstruction on existing FP4 hardware and inform the development of future MX-native inference systems.

title: Evaluating SAM-based and Convolutional Architectures in Thin Retinal Vessel Segmentation: Model Capacity, Computational Cost and Foundation Pre-training
summary: In retinal vessel segmentation, plain Vision Transformers (ViTs) are commonly expected to perform worse than convolutional neural networks (CNNs) on thin vessels, for reasons such as their coarse patch tokenization, their weak locality bias and their need for large training sets. Although this expectation is widely shared in the literature, how plain ViTs actually compare with CNNs on thin vessels has not been systematically quantified. We address this question by comparing a model with a plain ViT encoder (MedSAM), a hybrid Transformer (LiteMedSAM) and three CNNs of different sizes on three retinal datasets (DRIVE, HRF, FIVES) and, as a second-domain check, a microscopy dataset (VessMap). We measured the centerline recall and precision of thin vessels and compared the models while also considering their computational cost and how many epochs they needed to train. We found that the pre-trained MedSAM had a centerline recall of thin vessels that was not significantly different from that of the best CNN on all four datasets (-0.6 to +2.5 percentage points). A compact plain ViT obtained through architecture search but trained from scratch did not retain this performance. For pre-trained plain ViTs, our results do not support the expectation that they miss thin vessels, although similar thin-vessel performance can be obtained with much smaller models.

title: CalVLA: Shaping Native Confidence in Vision-Language-Action Policies with Outcome Supervision
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at the Science of Physical AI Safety (SPAIS) Workshop, CoRL 2026
summary: Can a vision-language-action (VLA) policy signal likely task failure from its own action probabilities? We introduce CalVLA, which shapes native action-token confidence using successful and failed rollouts and an Action-Confidence Alignment (ACal) squared margin-ranking loss. Low-rank adapters update OpenVLA-7B without an auxiliary failure detector. Observations are paired within tasks at similar normalized elapsed times, not necessarily equivalent physical progress. On a held-out test split from 500 LIBERO-10 configurations, adapted confidence achieves a joint failure-discrimination AUROC of $0.7392\pm0.0480$ over three seeds, averaging scores at 130 and 260 steps. Frozen-policy probes reach 0.6146--0.6436, but superiority over the linear probe is statistically inconclusive. For the same confidence summary, AUROC rises from 0.4485 before adaptation to 0.7327 after adaptation. Mean task success decreases from 58% to 55%. These results show improved failure discrimination, not improved control or established safety benefits.

title: Dependence-Aware Risk Assessment and Optimal Design of AI-Agent Safeguard Systems
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on safeguards to prevent unauthorized actions while preserving legitimate service. However, existing risk assessments often focus on individual safeguard performance while overlooking dependence among safeguard decisions. This paper develops a dependence-aware framework for risk assessment and optimal design of multi-component AI safeguard systems, jointly selecting configurations and operating policies for sequential layered screening and selective verification. We establish stochastic comparisons of layered-screening error probabilities and invocation costs under lower-orthant ordering. For selective verification, we characterize exactly which policies have error probabilities and review costs that respond monotonically to stronger dependence under supermodular ordering. For a fixed first stage and reviewer, we show that the optimal routing map is a two-threshold rule in the first-stage likelihood ratio. An accompanying open-source software package, Dependence-Aware Policy Optimization Algorithms (DAPOA), facilitates the practical implementation of the proposed framework. Numerical experiments show that ignoring dependence can lead to inaccurate risk assessments and infeasible safeguard designs, with independence-based selections violating security requirements in six of eight scenarios. An empirical study using four LLM safeguards on benchmark-derived agent actions further demonstrates the practical implications of dependence modeling. Under the principal operating setting, dependence-aware selection lowers held-out total cost by 39.6% relative to independence-based selection.

title: LF-VideoQA: Evaluating Long-Video Understanding with Long-Form Theory-of-Mind Questions
summary: The hardest part of understanding a long video is not pinpointing any one moment but synthesizing many, e.g., answering a question that requires tracking what develops across hours of content and articulating how the pieces fit together. To date, most long-video QA datasets require only a short answer or a multiple-choice selection, oversimplifying the long-video understanding task to retrieval. We introduce LF-VideoQA, a dataset for long-form, open-ended question answering over long narrative videos built on theory-of-mind questions: a character's belief depends on everything they have seen or been told, so each question demands assembling and reasoning from evidence distributed across the video. The dataset contains more than 6,300 questions on 94 recent films; each requires reasoning over scenes spanning an average of 23 minutes and comes with a question-specific rubric for recall and precision scoring. The dataset is created entirely automatically by annotating screenplays with scene events and each character's first-order beliefs and meta-beliefs, then generating (question, answer, rubric) triples through LLM-based question generation and verification; human studies validate their quality. We evaluate four families of state-of-the-art open-source VLMs across three settings and find the task highly challenging: (i) even an oracle with access to the screenplay falls well short of complete answers; (ii) the best non-oracle model attains barely half of the recall level of the oracle; (iii) unlike on prior long-video benchmarks, captions and subtitles underperform the video itself, indicating that the questions need visual evidence; and (iv) recall is the predominant bottleneck, with answers omitting many required rubric claims.

title: MoRE-GS: Motion-Regime Experts for Future Gaussian Splatting
summary:
Future dynamic novel-view synthesis requires extrapolating multiple motion regimes within the same scene. A single dynamics model may not simultaneously represent stationary regions, coordinated motion, local interactions, and articulated trajectories. We introduce Motion Regime Expert Routing for Gaussian Splatting (MoRE-GS), a causal, render-aware framework for forecasting dynamic 3D Gaussian scenes. MoRE-GS freezes a Gaussian representation reconstructed exclusively from the observed temporal prefix and forecasts its control-keypoint motion using four complementary experts: persistence, a coefficient-space Transformer, a graph convolutional network, and a structured Transformer with rigid and non-rigid motion constraints. A compact routing table assigns expert mixtures across soft motion groups and forecast-horizon bins, while a persistence gate suppresses unreliable extrapolation. Across D-NeRF and HyperNeRF scenes, MoRE-GS achieves improved performance against other methods, and these results demonstrate that renderer-calibrated composition of complementary motion predictors improves causal dynamic Gaussian forecasting across heterogeneous motion regimes.
  Project page: https://advanced-vision-and-learning-lab.github.io/MoRE-GS-website/

title: Unlearning by Extrapolating a Shrink-and-Heal Lookahead
summary: Unlearning aims to make a large language model behave like one retrained without its forget set. Prevailing likelihood-suppression objectives, however, lack an explicit forgetting target: they continually reward lower forget-set likelihood, making forgetting sensitive to the optimization budget. We address this limitation by estimating the direction toward the oracle without training it. Our key idea is to shrink the fine-tuned model toward its pre-fine-tuning weights and briefly re-learn the retain set, thereby removing the forget-specific contribution; in the linearized regime, this shrink-and-heal lookahead moves the model a fixed fraction of the way to the retrained model, its unique fixed point. Our method, SHIFT, extrapolates the lookahead's per-token changes into distillation targets and iteratively refines them. Evaluated against eleven baselines under a unified OpenUnlearning protocol, SHIFT achieves the highest aggregate score across all TOFU settings and the closest oracle alignment, 3.7x closer on average than the next-best method; on MUSE, it preserves the most retain knowledge. Under larger optimization budgets, baselines overshoot the oracle, while SHIFT remains near it, even under relearning attacks.

title: SIEVE: Preserving Cross-Image Evidence via Depth-Aware Token Compression
comment: 19 pages, including supplementary material. Code: https://github.com/nitishshukla86/SIEVE
summary: Multi-image vision-language models (VLMs) incur substantial computation when processing long visual sequences. Compressing these sequences must preserve complementary evidence across images and keep tokens from different images separate. Global selection can underrepresent question-relevant images, and pruning in early decoder layers risks removing relevant content before sufficient multimodal processing, yet existing methods spend most of the budget on these early layers. We propose SIEVE, a training-free, single-pass framework that jointly allocates visual tokens across images and decoder depth. SIEVE first pools each image into a compact spatial grid to reduce early processing cost. It then progressively selects representatives using prompt attention under equal per-image quotas and aggregates unselected tokens into similar representatives from the same image. These operations keep every image represented and its tokens separate from other images, while refining the retained representations. A closed-form schedule sets retention counts to target a prescribed average token budget across decoder layers. Across four VLM backbones, SIEVE achieves the highest average at a 6.25% budget on five multi-image benchmarks and four single-image benchmarks, and the highest mean on two video benchmarks. On LLaVA-OneVision-7B, it outperforms the strongest baseline by 9.96 and 9.03 points at 6.25% and 12.5% budgets, and at 12.5% it exceeds the uncompressed model by 2.01 points with 6.6x fewer prefill FLOPs.

title: On the Limits of Test-Time Compute for Self-Evaluation
summary: Self-verification and aggregation have emerged as popular approaches for bridging the gap between pass@1 and pass@N. However, increasing the number of candidates does not consistently narrow the gap between final-answer accuracy and pass@N. To understand this limitation, we use ranking error to measure how reliably models distinguish their correct generations from incorrect ones. We show that ranking error admits a bias-variance decomposition, with both components shaped by algorithmic design choices and inference compute. Across our experiments, additional compute reduces variance, while bias initially decreases before approaching a plateau. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Scorpio, a simple and general method that jointly scores randomly grouped candidates. Across math, code, and puzzle benchmarks, Scorpio improves verification, tree search, and aggregation. For verification, Scorpio improves accuracy over the strongest baseline by up to 7 percentage points while matching or exceeding that baseline's peak accuracy with 17-42% lower inference cost. For tree search, using Scorpio to score partial solutions and select the final answer improves accuracy by up to 10 percentage points over prior methods. Finally, Scorpio improves the scaling of aggregation-based methods by 11 percentage points on coding tasks.

title: DEPLOY-RL: Active Boundary Discovery and Conservative Certification for Deployable Reinforcement Learning in Safety-Critical Continuous Processes
comment: 8 pages; published in IJCAI-ECAI 2026, AI4Tech track. This version adds a publication notice
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) policies often outperform classical controllers in simulation, yet rarely reach production in safety-critical processes. The barrier is that there is no principled way to answer "Is this policy safe to deploy?" with statistical guarantees. We introduce DEPLOY-RL, a post-training certification framework built on one key insight: deployment certification requires discovering where failures occur (boundary discovery), not measuring how much everywhere (uniform reconstruction). Our contributions: (1) a contract-coupled acquisition function that concentrates sampling on certification-critical boundaries, achieving approximately 2x sample efficiency with a semi-empirical ambiguity reduction bound (domain-calibrated convergence guarantee); (2) conformal risk control providing finite-sample false-go guarantees (<= alpha) under explicit deployment contracts; (3) a three-way decision framework (Deploy/No-Deploy/Abstain) with fail-safe PID/MPC fallback. In simulations on papermaking (industrial digital twin) and Tennessee Eastman (public benchmark), DEPLOY-RL achieves 4.4% false-go rate (vs. 8.6% for the best baseline) while retaining 88.6% policy coverage, the only method achieving <5% false-go with >85% coverage among 14 baselines under our evaluation protocol.

title: Efficient NPN Classification for Large Functions using Graph Neural Network
summary: Two Boolean functions are considered NPN equivalent if one can be transformed into the other by negating inputs, permuting inputs, or negating the output. Efficient NPN classification is valuable in fields such as logic synthesis, quantum computing, and information theory. However, exact NPN classification demands exhaustive enumeration of all possible input permutations and negations. Its complexity grows exponentially, making it impractical for larger functions with more inputs. In this paper, we introduce the first learning-based formulation for NPN classification by recasting it as NPN action prediction. Our method represents Boolean functions as AND-Inverter Graphs (AIGs) and applies a bidirectional heterogeneous graph neural network to predict input negations, output negation, and input permutations. To mitigate the non-canonicity of logic networks, we further introduce graph rewriting techniques that reduce structural ambiguity and recover useful symmetries before prediction. Experimental results show that NPN action prediction is learnable, that the resulting canonicalization quality improves over heuristic baselines, and that on practical benchmarks our method approaches exact methods on tractable cases while scaling to functions with up to 16 inputs.

title: Decomposing Irregular Time Series into Interpretable Temporal Patterns with Mixture-of-Experts
summary: Irregularly-spaced sequential data, such as transaction logs, encode multi-scale temporal structure that is critical for prediction but difficult to recover explicitly with standard sequence models, which often trade interpretability for performance. We introduce MoTIF, an interpretable framework using mixture-of-experts (MoE) attention to decompose irregular time series into temporal patterns spanning minute-to-year scales. Each expert is trained via temporal alignment that induces attention specialization to a designated cyclical or within-range pattern, with label-free routing supervision that learns to activate the correct expert from patterns present in the data. On synthetic data with known temporal structure, MoTIF recovers correct routing well above chance (0.389/0.829 for range/cyclical patterns vs. 0.091 random) and outperforms all baselines, including a standard transformer and an unspecialized MoE, on next-value prediction. On a public credit card transaction dataset, MoTIF achieves higher macro-F1 than all baselines for next-amount prediction. Its learned routing reveals structure a black-box model cannot: transactions are governed primarily by intraday and short-interval rhythms, while fraudulent transactions show bursty, calendar-agnostic timing versus the steadier periodicity of legitimate ones. On downstream fraud detection, MoTIF matches standard transformer and MoE baselines and clearly outperforms recent sequential recommendation models used as embedding baselines. These results show that decomposing temporal structure into interpretable, expert-specific patterns need not sacrifice predictive accuracy, offering a practical route to sequence models that are both accurate and auditable in high-stakes settings. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MoTIF-82E4.

title: C3: Speech-Guided KV Retrieval for Long-Context SpeechLLM Inference
summary: Speech language models encode audio at a much higher rate than text, causing the KV cache to dominate the memory, bandwidth, and decoding cost of long-form generation. KV retrieval can reduce per-step access by attending to only a query-dependent subset of the cache, but existing methods are designed primarily for text and do not account for the structure of audio attention. We first show that retrieval errors may compound autoregressively into generation drift. We then analyze full audio attention during long-form generation and identify three properties relevant to retrieval: unequal attention concentration across query heads, non-contiguous audio support, and temporal continuity across decoding steps. Guided by these observations, we propose $C^3$(Cluster-Compete-Compete), which organizes audio KVs in a hierarchical key-space index, lets query heads sharing a KV head compete for a common retrieval budget, and adaptively reallocates retrieval resolution through paired split-merge updates. Across long-form speech recognition, translation, and summarization on four SpeechLLMs, $C^3$ achieves the strongest overall performance among retrieval methods under comparable final-KV access budgets, with particularly large gains in the tight-budget regime, while improving long-context decoding efficiency and accelerator-memory scaling.

title: Déjà Vu: Cycle-Consistent Re-ranking for Semantic Correspondence
summary: We propose \emph{Déjà Vu}, a test-time decoding module for semantic correspondence. Matching semantically equivalent keypoints across images of the same object category is challenging due to variations in appearance, viewpoint, and scale. While features from large pretrained vision models carry strong zero-shot correspondence ability, existing methods reduce final matching to greedy top-$1$ nearest-neighbor selection. We show that the correct correspondence appears among the top-ranked candidates far more often than top-$1$ matching achieves: with $30$ candidates, zero-shot features exceed the top-$1$ accuracy of a supervised model. This reveals a \textit{decoding bottleneck} rather than a limit of the representation. Motivated by this observation, we formulate semantic correspondence as a \textit{recall-then-rerank} problem. Our method first nominates an adaptive candidate set, larger when the similarity distribution is ambiguous and smaller when it is confident, then re-ranks the candidates with a graded cycle-consistency score: each candidate is matched back to the source image and penalized by how far its reverse match lands from the original keypoint. The module operates entirely on the similarity matrix already computed by the base method. It consistently improves three representative baselines on SPair-71k, its geometric subset, and PF-Pascal under both unsupervised and weakly supervised settings, with gains of up to $+1.8$ PCK@0.10 on SPair-71k and $+3.4$ PCK@0.15 on PF-Pascal, and $+4.9$ under Keypoint Average Precision.

title: Beyond Semantic IDs: Atomic Creator Tokens for Large-Scale Generative Recommendation
summary: Recommending creators that a user does not yet follow is a cold-start problem: from hundreds of thousands of popular creators and only a short trail of prior engagements, the system must predict the next creator worth surfacing. The prevailing generative recommendation recipe tokenizes each creator into a \emph{Semantic ID} (SID) by quantizing a frozen embedding and trains a language model to generate SIDs. We show that this SID layer, not the language model, is the binding constraint. The creator-to-SID map is many-to-one, so colliding creators must be resolved by a popularity tie-break that caps creator-level recall and favors already-popular creators, and the frozen quantizer stops the training gradient from reaching the creator representation. We propose Atomic Creator Token (ACT), which gives every creator its own vocabulary token trained end-to-end. The map is bijective, so collisions are impossible and inference is a direct top-$k$ over creator logits. In a controlled comparison on production data in which the token layer is the only variable, ACT improves creator-level Recall@15 by 19.8 points ($1.84\times$) over a matched SID baseline, still leads when the SID codebook is enlarged $64\times$, and serves at ${\sim}2.7\times$ lower per-user latency. The advantage carries over to the public KuaiRand dataset, where ACT is the only method that beats a global-popularity baseline, provided each creator token sees enough training examples. In a live A/B test, ACT is directionally positive on every reported metric against both the SID-enhanced and the classic production rankers.

title: Cyber-physical attack detection approaches in the wide-area measurement system
summary: Improving situational awareness within the Smart Grid is an effective preventive measure to detect potential anomalies, and avoid their adverse consequences. A wide area measurement system (WAMS) based Phasor Measurement Unit (PMU) can assist in improving visibility within the grid by collecting relevant measurements including magnitude, phase angle, frequency, voltage, and current, with a precise GPS-based timestamp. So far, there are more than 2500 PMUs deployed in the North American power grid, where each of which generates between 30 and 60 samples/s, roughly 1.5 TB/month of streamed data. Thus, processing such large PMU streams requires expensive computational resources and faster algorithms. This paper provides state-of-the-art cyber and physical anomalies in the WAMS and analyses their impact on the integrity and availability of the system. Next, it investigates the current anomaly detection approach in historical and streaming PMU data, including conventional machine learning and hybrid approaches, and assesses their advantages and main drawbacks. Lastly, it sheds light on the importance of handling missing PMU data and concept drifts.

title: Decentralized Multi-Agent Coordination and Communication in Shared Codebases
comment: First two authors contributed equally. Project Page: https://lingyunxiao18.github.io/ParallACT/
summary: Coding agents working in shared repositories may receive separate, independently-motivated requests from human developers, creating a setting that is multi-agent by necessity. When this scenario happens, their individual implementations may work separately but conflict when combined. To study this setting, we introduce ParallACT, a benchmark of orchestrator-free multi-agent coding tasks. ParallACT contains both complementary and contradictory tasks. In complementary tasks, each agent's task is separately useful and implementations must share an interface to be productively combined. In contradictory pairs, both agents' tasks require editing the same code in incompatible ways, and naively combining independent solutions fails to produce a useful implementation. We compare a single-agent oracle given the combined set of tasks against multi-agent settings that vary execution order, visibility, awareness of other agents, and access to a communication channel. We find that the oracle solves most tasks while parallel agents perform substantially worse. Their performance drop is notable for complementary tasks, and particularly sharp for contradictory tasks (e.g., from 62% to 16% for Claude Code with Claude Opus 4.8) where merged code typically satisfies only one specification, and the same gap appears in all six further configurations pairing two agent harnesses with three open-weight models. Simply telling an agent that a peer exists does not help significantly, and giving agents access to a communication channel recovers only a small part of the performance, at an additional token cost. ParallACT thus identifies and isolates a core challenge that will become more common as multi-agent coding by independent principals becomes standard, and provides a controlled test of which coordination strategies help, and at what cost.

title: RaMMOBO: Random Max-Margin Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization
summary: Multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) maximizes $M$ expensive black-box objectives with the goal of approximating the Pareto set, whose objective vectors cannot be improved in one component without sacrificing another. A common quality measure is hypervolume, the volume in objective space dominated by these vectors relative to a reference point. Expected hypervolume improvement (EHVI) directly targets this metric and is one-step Bayes-optimal, but its standard computation scales exponentially with $M$, making it prohibitively expensive for many-objective problems. We introduce random max-margin multi-objective Bayesian optimization (RaMMOBO), whose acquisition function lower-bounds EHVI while requiring only linear cost in $M$ to evaluate. RaMMOBO measures the volume of a max-margin box contained in a candidate's hypervolume-improvement region and averages over random reweightings of the objective space, yielding a utility that is strictly Pareto-monotone on hypervolume-improving outcomes. It naturally handles noisy observations and different probabilistic surrogates and supports efficient gradient-based optimization. Across synthetic and real-world benchmarks, RaMMOBO matches or outperforms state-of-the-art methods, with largest gains at higher $M$, with acquisition optimization up to two orders of magnitude faster than qLogNEHVI. Our implementation is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/rammobo.

title: A Framework for Task-Agnostic Counterfactual Fairness in Transformers through Activation Steering
summary: Bias in transformer-based models is a growing concern as these architectures become more prevalent in automated decision-making systems, such as prediction models for hiring, lending, and clinical treatment recommendation. Mechanistic interpretability (MI) is a growing body of work that measures meaningful causal effects of activations on model output by identifying human-interpretable features encoded in model activations. When such features correspond to sensitive attributes, they provide a direct way to quantify the bias those attributes introduce and to causally intervene to mitigate it. However, counterfactual fairness (CF) methods have not been systematically adapted to this setting of intervening on interpretable mechanisms in transformers. We propose a framework, Mechanistic Interpretability for Counterfactual Fairness (MICF), that utilizes MI tools to reformulate CF constraints in terms of transformer activations, unifying former approaches into a single pipeline for fairness analysis in transformers. MICF does not require a prior causal model or specific transformer architecture. We evaluate MICF on real-world tabular data and show that CF can be improved across different prediction tasks.

title: Seeing the Unseen: Unified Visible--Invisible Motion for Physically Consistent Video Generation
summary: Recent advances in video generation have achieved impressive visual quality, yet they often fail to produce physically consistent dynamics due to the lack of explicit modeling of underlying physical processes. Existing approaches either rely on simulators with strong assumptions or use coarse semantic guidance, and further struggle to effectively inject physical priors into generation models. In this work, we propose Seeing the Unseen, a unified framework for physics-grounded video generation. Our approach decomposes the problem into two stages: learning physical dynamics and injecting them into video synthesis. First, we introduce a lightweight Particle-based Graph Dynamics Simulator (PGDS) that learns generalizable physical interactions from data and predicts plausible 3D motion trajectories. Second, we propose a Visible--Invisible Motion Field (VIMF) that captures both motion observable in the input frame and motion that emerges over time due to object dynamics. This representation enables more complete and structured motion guidance compared to conventional physical signals. By integrating these trajectories into a diffusion-based generator, our method produces videos that are both visually coherent and physically consistent. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved motion accuracy, interaction consistency, and reduced physical artifacts compared to strong baselines.

title: Quantifying Local and Global Fidelity of Nonlinear Embeddings
summary: Dimension reduction methods are chosen by a common claim: t-SNE and UMAP preserve local structure, and PCA preserves global structure. Checking it on given data takes local and global scores on one scale and a test that compares two maps. Both scores come from one curve. The locality profile is the chance-corrected share of each point's k nearest neighbors that a map keeps, over all neighborhood sizes. Its value at k = 10 is the local fidelity L, and its mean over 30 to 50 percent of the data is the global fidelity G. We prove that at the midpoint the profile is the agreement on which half of the data is near each point, a rank correlation of the distances. Because L and G are one statistic, two maps can be tested against each other. The LG reversal test applies to any two dimension reduction methods. It decides, with a block-jackknife p-value, whether one map is more local and the other more global, and returns the scale at which to change maps. On 156 maps of twelve datasets with up to 1.38 million points, G agrees with established global scores at 0.89 and 0.96, and 2,000 points estimate it. The test confirms the usual claim on seven datasets. On both retail datasets and both rolled-up manifolds, it finds the neighbor embeddings more global.
